top.title: HSBC profits surge 32%, sparking fresh calls for bank taxes in the budget – business live
top.summary: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news The TUC are also urging the Chancellor to increase taxes on banks in tomorrow’s Budget, arguing the sector could pay tens of billions of pounds more. Rather than simply reversing Jeremy Hunt’s cut to the bank surcharge from 8% to 3%, the TUC argue that the surcharge – additional corporation tax – should be increased further. “Some in the finance lobby have tried every which way to stop tax rises in the Budget. But these results make it blatantly obvious banks can afford to contribute more. “It’s not just HSBC. Barclays announced bumper profits last week too. And Britain’s big four banks have made more than £200bn in profit over the last five years. “It’s not surprising that HSBC have made such significant profits in the last quarter, but it will be difficult news to swallow for households struggling with rising mortgage costs. Like other big banks, its profitability has depended on keeping interest rates on savings accounts low, and a “stealth subsidy” from taxpayers via the Bank of England due to quantitative easing. “While the rumours of a bank tax change in the Budget are welcome, it is unlikely to go far enough. While banks are making over a billion pounds a week of profit, NEF analysis suggests that the restoration of the bank surcharge to 8% would raise just £1.8bn a year from them.The chancellor should go further by clawing back the stealth subsidy, and use this to fund inflation-busting investment and keep the essentials of life affordable for ordinary people.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: Our loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighbours
Culture.summary: A low-budget building by the Olympic site that was never meant to last has been given a £4m revamp full of Italian pizzazz. Now The Yard is putting bums on (heated) seats – and Ian McKellen is soon to star Since the 2012 Olympics, the skyline of Hackney Wick in east London has bristled with cranes. The athletes may be long gone but the legacy of the sporting spectacle rolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape. But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of the Yard theatre . Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below. Continue reading...
